steps.body: The all-purpose continuous model: **A = P·e^(rt)** — P the start, r the continuous rate (negative for decay), t the time. $500 at 6% for 10 years: A = 500·e^0.6 ≈ 500 · 1.822 = **$911**. Algebra 1's a·bˣ models, upgraded to compound every instant.

widget.prompt: A = 200·e^(0.05·20) = 200·e¹. e is not a round number, so slide the base until b¹ lands near 2.7 — the finest step this dial reaches.
widget.successFeedback: This dial's best step is 2.7; e itself is 2.71828…, close enough that the two agree to two places. Using the lesson's own e ≈ 2.718, the growth factor is 200 × 2.718 ≈ 544 — the widget shows WHY the number lands near 2.7-and-a-bit, without pretending a dial in tenths can reach an irrational number exactly.
widget.lowFeedback: Still below e — the growth factor has not caught up to 2.7 yet.
widget.highFeedback: Past e now — the dial has gone beyond 2.7.

steps.body: Read the anatomy: in A = 300·e^(0.08t), the start is **300** (t = 0 makes e⁰ = 1) and the continuous rate is **8%**. A negative rate flips it to decay: A = P·e^(−0.10t) shrinks continuously at 10%. Same skeleton either way — the exponent's sign tells the story.

explanationVariants: At t = 0: A = 450 · e⁰ = 450; the exponent's coefficient 0.03 is the rate: 3%.
Coefficient = start; exponent coefficient = continuous rate.

widget.prompt: For A = 450·e^(0.03t), the starting amount and continuous rate are:

options.label: 450 and 3%
options.feedback: Right — e⁰ = 1 exposes the 450; 0.03 as a percent is 3%.

options.label: 450 and 0.03%
options.feedback: The DECIMAL 0.03 converts to 3 percent — two decimal places over.

options.label: 0.03 and 450%
options.feedback: The big number out front is the START; the small exponent coefficient is the rate.

options.label: 453 and 3%
options.feedback: At t = 0 nothing has grown yet: A = 450 exactly, not 450 + 3.

widget.prompt: When does $500 at 7% continuous growth reach $1000? Solve 2 = e^(0.07t) using ln 2 ≈ 0.693 (one decimal).

commonErrors.feedback: t = (ln 2)/0.07 = 0.693/0.07 ≈ 9.9 — dividing by 0.0485 or similar misreads the rate.
Divide ln 2 BY the rate: 0.693/0.07 ≈ 9.9 years (0.14 inverts the division).

explanationVariants: P cancels in P·e^(rt) = 2P — the doubling time t = (ln 2)/r never sees the starting amount.
Big or small principal, same doubling clock.

widget.prompt: How does the doubling time of A = P·e^(rt) depend on the starting amount P?

options.label: It does not depend on P; P cancels from the doubling equation
options.feedback: Right — $5 and $5 million double on the same schedule at equal rates.

options.label: A larger P doubles faster because it starts farther ahead
options.feedback: Divide both sides of Pe^(rt) = 2P by P — it vanishes; only the rate r sets the clock.

options.label: A larger P doubles slower because it takes more to double
options.feedback: The P cancels from the equation entirely — doubling time is (ln 2)/r, rate-only.

options.label: Only P matters; the rate r does not set the doubling time
options.feedback: Exactly backwards: t = (ln 2)/r depends on r ALONE.

explanationVariants: e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.607 — more than half survives (continuous 25% for 2 units isn't 50% gone).

widget.prompt: A sample decays continuously: A = 600·e^(−0.25·2). Using e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.607, what is A to the nearest whole?

commonErrors.feedback: e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.607, not 0.5 — continuous decay leaves MORE than the naive half: ≈ 364.
236 is what was LOST (600 − 364) — A asks what REMAINS: 600 · 0.607 ≈ 364.

explanationVariants: Isolate, ln, divide by the TIME to expose the rate.

widget.prompt: $300 grows continuously to $450 in 5 years: 450 = 300·e^(5r). Using ln 1.5 ≈ 0.405, find r as a percent (one decimal).

commonErrors.feedback: Divide ln 1.5 by the 5 YEARS: 0.405/5 = 0.081 → 8.1% (40.5 skips that division).
The naive (150/300)/5 = 10% ignores compounding — continuously, only ln 1.5/5 ≈ 8.1% is needed.

steps.body: A = Pe^(rt): e evaluates forward, ln solves backward.
takeaways: Coefficient = start; exponent coefficient = continuous rate (sign = direction).
Doubling time (ln 2)/r ignores the principal entirely.
'How long?' and 'what rate?' are both one ln away.
steps.teaser: Next: half-life — decay's version of the doubling clock.

concept.body: The model at t = 0: A = 900·e^(0.04·0), and e⁰ = 1.

explanationVariants: No time elapsed, no growth — the coefficient is the start.

widget.prompt: For A = 900·e^(0.04t), what is A at t = 0?

commonErrors.feedback: At t = 0 the exponent is 0 and e⁰ = 1 — no growth yet: exactly 900.
The EXPONENT is 0; the amount is 900 · 1 = 900.
